explanations.explanation: It appears this feature is signaling and “steering” the model’s handling of hyphenated compounds or multi‐word expressions. When the feature is active, the model correctly predicts the second part of a compound adjective (as in “low‐fat” or “high‐speed”), whereas without it the next token degenerates into a fragment (“ck” or “head”) that reflects a mis‐segmentation. In short, it represents the awareness and proper processing of hyphenated compound word constructions.

It appears that this feature “fires” on the beginnings of styled, headline‐or announcement–type phrases—fragments that look like the start of titles (e.g. “Prim…”, “Immun…”, “Ep…”, “Cong…”, “Join…”) that cue the model into a formal, celebratory or event‐announcement mode. In short, the feature signals a header or title “trigger” that shifts the next‐token distribution toward a continuation in that genre (where its absence leads to a generic “otherwise”), indicating it’s capturing the stylistic and contextual mark of such proclamative introductions.

This feature activates when the model identifies that a token is part of a compound or morphologically bound form (such as a hyphenated connection or an adjective‐forming suffix). In other words, it signals that the token is not standalone but is joining together pieces of a word or phrase—which in turn shifts next-token predictions to complete or extend that compound construction.

It appears that this feature signals a compound‐or hyphenated morpheme boundary. In other words, it activates when the model is encoding a compound word or segmented term (often split by an explicit hyphen or implicit sub‐morpheme break, as in “dead‐on,” “ched‐dar,” “cutting‐edge,” etc.), and it influences the subsequent token prediction accordingly.

explanations.explanation: It appears this feature is attuned to detecting abbreviation markers—especially the kinds found in proper names or titles (such as a middle initial followed by a period) that signal an abbreviated element in a named entity before a new token (often an uppercase letter) begins.

The feature is not about a semantic topic but a learned punctuation/word‐boundary signal—it “fires” when the model sees what looks like an abbreviated term (for example the period following “Gov”) or an otherwise completed word token. In those cases it cues the model to treat the word as finished so that the next token is predicted appropriately (rather than “completing” the current token with extra letters).

It’s picking out the “tail‐piece” of a split, morphologically complex word—that is, the feature fires when the token is the final segment (a suffix or particle like “‑ided”, “‑uded”, “‑lessly”, “up”, “‑ered”, even punctuation in abbreviations or compounds) that signals a compound or phrasal verb construction. This snippet “carries” information about the word’s inflected or multi‐word structure that the model uses to predict the following token.

It appears this feature is tracking a particular morphemic “chunk” that signals a shift from a connected to a disconnected state – in other words, it “fires” on word‐pieces like “plug”, “def” (as in “redefining”), “inhib” (in “uninhibited”), and similar segments found in terms for plugging/unplugging, recharging, or otherwise altering a state. This pattern seems to help the model distinguish contexts where a physical or metaphorical connection (and its subsequent disconnection or reset) is in play.

It’s a feature that “flags” the opening sub‐piece of a common multi–token expression—often a proper‐name or a contraction (e.g. the “Secret(ary)” in “Secretary of State” or the “Don(’t)” in advice phrases)—so that the model treats these as a unit with a highly specific continuation. In short, it encodes an orthographic/morphological cue for institutional/quoted phrases and negation contractions that strongly conditions the following token.

explanations.explanation: It detects when the context calls for a “reference‐style” token—that is, a proper numeral, model name, version, license or section identifier embedded in formal or technical text. In such cases the feature pushes the distribution toward a specific, non–generic proper noun rather than a common filler token.

It appears that the feature detects sentence‐end (or boundary) punctuation – a marker (often a period) that signals you’ve finished one syntactic/discourse unit and are about to start another. This boundary signal shifts the next‐token distribution toward sentence‐initial or transition words (e.g. “since,” “accused,” “Journal,” “President”), making it a core controller of sentence segmentation and subsequent context shifts.

It detects a subword‐chunk that signals a compound modifier—often one formed with a hyphen or split across morphemes (as in “built‐in” or the “int” in “ointment” or “ky” in “quirky”)—which marks an integrated, modified quality in descriptive product or feature language.

The feature appears to be a marker for internal word‐structure: it highlights subword or affix segments—especially in compound words, multi‐language names, technical identifiers, or other “nonstandard” tokens—that signal their proper continuation (and hence affect the next-token prediction).

It’s the model’s “ornamental‐glyph” detector—it fires when text is decorated with unusual or extra Unicode symbols used for style or emphasis (for example in ads or stylized headings), which in turn shifts the next-token prediction from ordinary letters (like “e”) to that special glyph.

This feature appears to capture when a token is not the start of a whole word but instead a sub‐unit—a morpheme or continuation segment—that attaches to a preceding piece. In other words, it signals a word’s “internal” part (often in names, compounds, or hyphenated terms), influencing how the next token is predicted by marking that the current subword is incomplete.

This feature signals an abbreviation‐ending period—a punctuation token occurring right after a shortened or truncated proper noun or term—which cues the model to treat the preceding token as an abbreviation and adjust its next-token prediction accordingly.

It appears that this feature is keying in on abbreviated expressions—that is, a short, capitalized token (often a title or initial) immediately followed by a period. In these contexts (e.g. “Gov.”, “James M.”, “Andrew J.”, “ST. …”) the feature signals that an abbreviation or name‐initial is ending, thereby affecting the next token prediction.

It’s a signal that a subword piece is not a “word‐start” at all but an internal, morphologically or orthographically “glued‐on” segment (an affix or compound fragment) whose presence biases the language model toward a particular continuation that maintains the intended internal word structure.
It’s a feature that lights up on sentence‐final punctuation—especially periods—marking a sentence boundary and signaling a reset in context that shifts the model’s next-token expectations.
